```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# load a few R packages
library(here)
library(knitr)

# for table fits
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
	library(flextable)
})

fit_flextable_to_page <- function(tbl, page_width = 6.5){
	
	ft_out <- tbl |> flextable::autofit()
	
	ft_width <- (dim(ft_out)$widths * page_width) /
		(flextable::flextable_dim(ft_out)$widths)
	
	ft_out <- flextable::width(ft_out, width = ft_width)
	
	return(ft_out)
}
```

# Reproducibility instructions

Our data and code are archived on GitHub (https://github.com/ahgroup/john-norovirus-antibody-kinetics-public) and Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19799472). To reproduce our results, first clone or download the GitHub repository. Once downloaded, open the `.Rproj` file in RStudio. We used the R package `targets` [@zotero-item-38674] to implement the analysis pipeline which can be executed in full by running `targets::tar_make()`. The pipeline automatically detects the number of cores on your device and runs in parallel, leaving two cores free. For reproducibility across devices, model fitting was parallelized adaptively based on available system resources. The total number of available CPU cores was determined while leaving two cores free, and each model was assigned approximately one quarter of the remaining cores (with at least one core per model) for MCMC sampling. This approach ensures that total core usage remains bounded while enabling efficient parallel computation across different computing environments. Note that parallel execution may be resource-intensive on personal computers; if you are in a limited computing environment, you can run sequentially by specifying `use_crew = FALSE`. However, running all Bayesian models sequentially may be very slow. You can visualize the workflow using `targets::tar_visnetwork()` and run only selected targets by passing a vector of target names to `tar_make()`, optionally using tidyselect helpers. Due to OS and file system differences, some targets may appear outdated even when up-to-date; this can be safely ignored. Note that not all model result files are included in the GitHub repository, as they exceed 10GB. To inspect or modify the Bayesian models, you will need to rerun the code.

Once you have cloned our repository, follow these instructions to reproduce our results.

1. Open the `john-norovirus-antibody-kinetics-public.Rproj` file in RStudio.
2. Once renv initializes, run the command renv::restore() in the console to begin installing the required packages. If you have issues at this stage you can also install the dependencies manually, but if you do not use renv or you use different package versions than we did, our code might not work for you.
3. If you want to run any steps that involve Bayesian models, you need to install cmdstanr following the cmdstanr quick start guide at this location: https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html. We used cmdstanr version 2.38.0 for this project [@jonah_gabry_cmdstanr_2025].
4.	Now you can run our pipeline by running `targets::tar_make()` in the console. If you would like to run only the main text results, run `targets::tar_make("reproduce_manuscript")` in the console. See the `_targets.R` file for further instructions and the full pipeline. If you are new to targets and want to learn more about how the pipeline works, we recommend reading the targets manual which can be found here: https://books.ropensci.org/targets/.

We conducted all analyses in R version 4.5.2 (2025-10-31 ucrt) [@zotero-item-38678] in RStudio version 2026.01.0+392 [@zotero-item-38677]. The full pipeline, including supplementary analyses, took us approximately 17 hours to run. Reproducing only the main text analyses took us approximately 6 hours.

# Extended methods

## Model formulation

### Antibody induction model

The initial antibody response was modeled using a sigmoid function describing antibody concentration over time. The equation is given by

$$\mu(t) = \frac{P}{1+\exp(-G \cdot (t-K))}$$

where:

-   $P$ is the asymptotic amplitude of the induction term,

-   $G$ is the growth rate, and

-   $K$ is the inflection point at which the induction term reaches 50% of its asymptote.

To ensure biologically plausible trajectories, models were fit on the natural logarithmic scale, and parameters were exponentiated within the model to ensure positivity. To account for individual variation, the model for an individual $i$ at time $t$, denoted $\eta_{i,t}$, becomes:

$$\eta_{i,t} = \frac{\exp(p_i)}{1+\exp(-\exp(g_i)\cdot(t-\exp(k_i)))}$$

where $P = \exp(p_i)$, $G = \exp(g_i)$, and $K = \exp(k_i)$.

### Antibody decay models

We implemented two decay models: exponential and power-law. The exponential model assumes a constant rate of decay, whereas the power-law model allows the decay rate to slow over time, which may better reflect long-term immune memory dynamics. In both models, the decay parameter is denoted by $D_i$.

Exponential decay model: 

$$\exp(-D_1 \cdot t)$$

Power-law decay model: 

$$t^{-D_2}$$

Because the power-law function is undefined at $t=0$, we shift the time scale by one unit by replacing $t$ with $t+1$ to avoid singularities. As with the induction phase, the decay parameter is exponentiated to ensure positivity such that $D = \exp(d_i)$. Subject-specific random effects on $d_i$ capture individual variation in decay.

### Full generative models

The full models were constructed as the product of the induction and decay components, expressed on the log scale. Let $\eta_{i,t}$ denote the mean log antibody level for individual $i$ at time $t$.

Exponential decay model:

$$\eta_{i,t} = \log \left( \frac{\exp(p_{i_1})}{1+\exp(-\exp(g_{i_1})\cdot(t-\exp(k_{i_1})))} \cdot \exp(-\exp(d_{i_1}) \cdot t) \right)$$

Power-law decay model:

$$\eta_{i,t} = \log \left( \frac{\exp(p_{i_2})}{1+\exp(-\exp(g_{i_2})\cdot((t+1)-\exp(k_{i_2})))} \cdot (t+1)^{-\exp(d_{i_2})} \right)$$

## Statistical model specification

### Likelihood and hierarchical structure

Models were implemented in a Bayesian hierarchical framework. Antibody measurements were modeled on the log scale using a Student-$t$ likelihood to accommodate heavy-tailed biological variation and outliers. The degrees of freedom parameter $v$ was fixed at 4, and the residual scale parameter $\sigma$ was assigned a Half-Student-$t(3,0,2)$ prior.

$$\text{log}(y_{i,t}) \sim \text{Student}(v=4,\eta_{i,t},\sigma)$$

$$\sigma \sim \text{Half-Student}(3,0,2)$$

The expected antibody trajectory $\eta_{i,t}$ was defined by the kinetic functions described above. Dose level was included as a categorical predictor using a cell-means parameterization, allowing each dose group to have its own population-level kinetic parameters $p_{dose_i}, g_{dose_i}, k_{dose_i}, d_{dose_i}$. We modeled individual-level variation using additive random effects on the latent parameter scale. We modeled random effects for each parameter as zero-centered normal deviations with parameter-specific standard deviations.

### Prior specification for kinetic parameters

Nonlinear kinetic models can exhibit weak parameter identifiability, particularly when estimating multiple trajectory parameters. We therefore used biologically motivated priors to regularize biologically implausible trajectories while allowing the observed data to inform posterior inference. Priors were selected based on expected antibody response magnitudes and biological timescales rather than diffuse priors that could permit unrealistic kinetic behavior.

The peak parameter was assigned $p \sim \text{Normal}(7,2)$ on the log scale. Because the model uses $\exp(p)$ as the peak response magnitude, this corresponds to a log-normal prior on the original scale with a median peak response of $\exp(7)\approx1,100$ units and an approximate 95% interval of approximately 22 to 55,000 units.

The growth parameter was assigned $g \sim \text{Normal}(0,1.5)$ on the log scale. This corresponds to a log-normal prior on the original scale with a median growth rate of 1 and an approximate 95% prior interval of 0.05 to 19.

The time-to-peak parameter was assigned $k \sim \text{Normal}(\log(10),1)$. This corresponds to a log-normal prior on the original scale with a median expected time scale of 10 days, with an approximate 95% prior interval of 1.4 to 72 days.

The decay parameter was assigned separate priors for each model because it has different interpretations under the exponential and power-law formulations. For the exponential model, $d_{1} \sim \text{Normal}(-4,1.5)$, corresponds to a median decay rate of 0.018 and an approximate 95% prior interval of 0.001 to 0.35. For the power-law model, $d_{2} \sim \text{Normal}(-1,1.5)$ corresponds to a log-normal prior on the power-law exponent with a median value of 0.37 and an approximate 95% prior interval of 0.02 to 4.65.

Random effect standard deviations were assigned Half-Student-$t(3,0,2)$ priors. Prior distributions were evaluated by comparing prior and posterior parameter distributions (@fig-prior-sens-1 - @fig-prior-sens-16).

### Exponential decay model

Time-series equation:

$$\eta_{i,t} = \log \left( \frac{\exp(p_{i_1})}{1+\exp(-\exp(g_{i_1})\cdot(t-\exp(k_{i_1})))} \cdot \exp(-\exp(d_{i_1}) \cdot t) \right)$$
Parameter definitions:

$$p_{i_1} = p_{0,i} + p_{1,dose_i}$$

$$g_{i_1} = g_{0,i} + g_{1,dose_i}$$

$$k_{i_1} = k_{0,i} + k_{1,dose_i}$$

$$d_{i_1} = d_{0,i} + d_{1,dose_i}$$

Random effects:

$$p_{0,i}, g_{0,i}, k_{0,i}, d_{0,i} \sim \text{Normal}(0, \gamma_{\cdot})$$

with group-level scales:

$$\sigma_p, \sigma_g, \sigma_k, \sigma_d \sim \text{Half-Student}(3,0,2)$$
Dose effects:

$$p_{1,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(7,2)$$

$$g_{1,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(0,1.5)$$

$$k_{1,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(\log(10),1)$$

$$d_{1,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(-4,1.5)$$

### Power-law decay model

Time-series equation:

$$\eta_{i,t} = \log \left( \frac{\exp(p_{i_2})}{1+\exp(-\exp(g_{i_2})\cdot((t+1)-\exp(k_{i_2})))} \cdot (t+1)^{-\exp(d_{i_2})} \right)$$

Parameter definitions:

$$p_{i_2} = p_{0,i} + p_{2,dose_i}$$

$$g_{i_2} = g_{0,i} + g_{2,dose_i}$$

$$k_{i_2} = k_{0,i} + k_{2,dose_i}$$

$$d_{i_2} = d_{0,i} + d_{2,dose_i}$$

Random effects:

$$p_{0,i}, g_{0,i}, k_{0,i}, d_{0,i} \sim \text{Normal}(0, \gamma_{\cdot})$$

with group-level scales:

$$\gamma_p, \gamma_g, \gamma_k, \gamma_d \sim \text{Half-Student}(3,0,2)$$

Dose effects:

$$p_{2,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(7,2)$$

$$g_{2,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(0,1.5)$$

$$k_{2,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(\log(10),1)$$

$$d_{2,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(-1,1.5)$$

## Model implementation

### Computation

Models were implemented using the `brms` package [@burkner2021a], which uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) implemented via Stan, to draw posterior samples of the model parameters. Each model was fit with 3,000 iterations per chain, including 1,000 warm-up iterations and 2,000 post-warmup samples. With four parallel Markov chains, this resulted in a total of 8,000 posterior samples per model. An adaptive delta of 0.99 was used to reduce divergent transitions, and the maximum tree depth was set to 15, corresponding to a maximum of $2^{15}=32,768$ leapfrog steps per iteration. We used the default values for all other algorithm parameters.

### Censoring

Censoring rules were defined based on assay characteristics, prior literature, and observed clusters in the data. For HBGA-blocking measurements, the assay detection range was 25 to 3200. In the NI study, the lower limits of detection were 0.8 for IgA and 0.7 for IgG, whereas in the NV study they were 3.1 for IgA and 1.6 for IgG. Observations at or above the upper detection limit were treated as right-censored, and those at or below the lower detection limit were treated as interval-censored, with lower bounds set to $10^{-6}$ and upper bounds equal to the assay-specific detection limit. The lower bound of $10^{-6}$ was chosen to avoid undefined values on the log scale, as antibody levels are strictly positive. Censoring was directly incorporated into the likelihood using the censored-response functionality of the Bayesian models implemented in brms, allowing both right- and interval-censored observations to contribute appropriately to posterior inference. The number of censored observations by antibody, dose, and collection timepoint is reported for the NI study (@tbl-ni-cens-GI1-HBGA-4p8 - @tbl-ni-cens-GI1-IgG-4800) and the NV study (@tbl-nv-cens-GI1-HBGA-5 - @tbl-nv-cens-GII4-IgG-150).

## Model assessment

A total of 16 models were fit, stratified by study, antibody, and decay function. We compared the parameter distributions under the original and broader prior specifications in @fig-prior-sens-1 - @fig-prior-sens-16. These figures also show the corresponding posterior distributions under each prior specification and illustrate how the observed data updated the priors. Figures showing only the implemented priors and corresponding posterior distributions were also generated and are available in the Github repository. Model performance was further supported by fitted-versus-observed plots (@fig-ni-fitted-observed, @fig-nv-fitted-observed). The fitted values generally captured the overall range and temporal pattern of the observed responses.

### Pairwise posterior distributions

Pairwise posterior parameter distributions are shown in @fig-ni-pairwise-pow-1 - @fig-nv-pairwise-pow-17. To conserve space, we show the power-law model for all antibodies in the 4.8-dose group in the NI study and the 5-dose group in the NV study as representative examples. Pairwise posterior distributions for all other study, antibody, dose, and decay-function combinations are available in the associated GitHub repository and can be reproduced using the analysis code.

Posterior correlation was observed between the growth rate ($g$) and inflection point ($k$) parameters across most models. In several models, peak magnitude ($p$) and decay rate ($d$) also showed posterior correlation. We conducted a sensitivity analysis using the observed data and found that observed peak and growth rate were negatively associated (@fig-ni-obs-peakday-growth, @fig-nv-obs-peakday-growth), and that observed peak value and decay rate were positively associated (@fig-ni-obs-peak-decay, @fig-nv-obs-peak-decay), as reflected in the pairwise posterior distributions. We can not rule out that these parameter dependencies partially reflect the model structure, but the observed data support the observed associations. These parameter dependencies did not prevent model convergence.

### Model comparison

We compared exponential and power-law decay models using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) based on the expected log predictive density (ELPD) [@mcelreath2020; @sivula2025]. Model performance was assessed using the difference in expected log predictive density between models, defined as

$$\Delta ELPD = ELPD_{power-law} - ELPD_{exponential}$$

Positive values of $\Delta ELPD$ indicate better predictive performance of the power-law model relative to the exponential model.

We obtained an estimate of the standard error of $\Delta ELPD$ from the approximate LOO-CV procedure. In small sample settings, the uncertainty of $\Delta ELPD$ may be underestimated due to the instability of pointwise predictive contributions [@sivula2025]. To address this, we applied a conservative adjustment by inflating the standard error by a factor of two, following a heuristic for uncertainty quantification in small samples [@bengio2003]:

$$\tilde{\sigma}_{\Delta} = 2 \cdot SE(\Delta ELPD)$$

To quantify the probability that the power-law model has better predictive performance than the exponential model, we approximated the sampling distribution of $\Delta ELPD$ using a normal distribution:

$$\Delta ELPD \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{\Delta}, \tilde{\sigma}^2_{\Delta})$$

where $\mu_{\Delta}$ is the estimated $\Delta ELPD$ and $\tilde{\sigma}_{\Delta}$ is the inflated standard error.

The probability that the power-law model is better than the exponential model is then given by:

$$P(\Delta ELPD > 0) = 1 - \Phi(0 | \mu_\Delta, \tilde{\sigma}_{\Delta})$$

Values of $P(\Delta ELPD > 0)$ close to 1 indicate strong support for the power-law model and values close to 0 indicate support for the exponential model.

## Posterior prediction and kinetic summaries

### Population- and individual-level trajectories

To visualize and summarize population-level antibody response trajectories following infection or vaccination, posterior predictions were generated over a finely spaced grid of time points. Time was discretized into two intervals: from day 0 to day 20 at 4-hour (1/6 day) intervals to capture early antibody induction dynamics, and from day 20 to day 400 at daily intervals to capture longer-term trajectories. Predictions were generated for all dose groups within each study.

Population-level posterior predictions of the natural log-transformed antibody response were obtained using `brms::posterior_epred()` with `re_formula=NA`, excluding subject-specific random effects. For each time point and dose group, posterior summaries were calculated using `brms::posterior_summary()` with robust estimation, yielding 95% equal-tailed credible intervals (CIs).

Individual-level antibody trajectories were generated using the same approach while retaining subject-specific random effects (`re_formula=NULL`), producing conditional predictions for each participant.

### Derived kinetic measures

We derived several antibody kinetics measures from the modeled trajectories, as illustrated in @fig-measures-schematic and described below. All kinetic summaries were calculated from posterior draws of the group-level trajectories. Individual-level random effects were incorporated during model fitting to account for participant-level variability but were not included in these summaries.

```{r}
#| label: fig-measures-schematic
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
knitr::include_graphics(here::here('results/figures/supplement/measures-schematic/measures-schematic.png'))
```

*Peak magnitude and time*

For each posterior draw, the modeled antibody trajectory was evaluated to identify the maximum titer and the time at which it occurred. Posterior medians and 95% CIs were computed to summarize group-level uncertainty.

*Peak response relative to baseline*

To assess the contribution of pre-existing antibodies, peak response relative to baseline was defined, for each posterior draw, as the difference between the estimated peak and baseline titers. Posterior medians and 95% CIs were used to summarize uncertainty.

*Early growth rate to peak*

The rate of antibody increase following exposure was estimated for each posterior draw by identifying the time at which the modeled titer reached 50% of its peak value on the original scale, using linear interpolation between points on the prediction grid. The growth rate was then calculated as the slope of the log-transformed titer trajectory between the two grid points bracketing this value to capture the early exponential increase phase. Growth rates are reported per day, and posterior medians with 95% CIs summarize uncertainty.

*Antibody decay rate*

Antibody waning was quantified as the change in modeled, natural log-transformed titer over one-day intervals centered at 60, 90, 180, and 365 days post-exposure. Multiple evaluation time points were used for the power-law model because decay is time-varying. Only one decay rate is reported for the exponential model, which assumes a constant decay rate.

*Predicted titer at 1 year*

Predicted titer at one year was defined as the posterior-predicted antibody titer at day 365. Posterior medians and 95% CIs were computed across draws.

*Persistence relative to baseline at 1 year*

To quantify antibody persistence relative to pre-existing immunity, predicted titer difference at one year was defined, for each posterior draw, as the difference between the predicted titer at day 365 and the baseline titer. Posterior medians and 95% CIs were summarized across draws.

### Pairwise dose comparisons of kinetic measures

To quantify dose-dependent differences in antibody kinetics, we computed posterior probabilities of pairwise dose comparisons for each kinetic measure, antibody type, and study. For each group, we extracted posterior draws for each dose and formed all ordered pairs. Draws were matched by MCMC iteration, and comparisons were computed using paired posterior draws. Any draws with missing values for a given comparison were omitted from that comparison. For each dose pair (i, j), we estimated the posterior probability that the measure at dose i exceeded that at dose j as the proportion of paired draws in which the value at dose i was greater:

$$\text{Pr}(\text{dose}_i > \text{dose}_j) = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^{S}{\theta_i^{(s)} > \theta_j^{(s)}}$$

where $\theta^{(s)}$ denotes the $s$-th posterior draw and $S$ is the total number of paired draws.  Results are presented as heatmaps (@fig-ni-pow-measure-probabilities and @fig-nv-pow-measure-probabilities). We report each pairwise comparison in one direction only; the reverse follows as $P(dose_j > dose_i) = 1 − P(dose_i > dose_j)$, such that all pairwise information is retained.

### Area under antibody trajectory

As a complementary summary of antibody kinetics, we calculated the area under the model-estimated antibody trajectory (AUC) from day 0 to one year after infection or vaccination. The AUC summarizes cumulative antibody levels over the first year and therefore reflects the combined effects of antibody induction and subsequent waning. For each posterior draw, the AUC was calculated using the trapezoidal rule. Predicted antibody levels below 1 were truncated to 1 prior to integration to avoid values below the assumed baseline. Posterior median AUCs and 95% credible intervals are shown alongside peak response, decay rate, and one-year response in @fig-auc-ni and @fig-auc-nv.

### IgA-to-IgG response ratios

To evaluate whether exposure type or dose influenced the relative induction of IgA and IgG responses, we calculated the ratio of model-estimated peak IgA response to peak IgG response for each dose group (@tbl-ni-iga-igg - @tbl-nv-iga-igg). Ratios were calculated using posterior draws from the group-level model estimates and summarized as posterior medians with 95% credible intervals. Ratios greater than 1 indicate a greater modeled peak IgA response relative to IgG, whereas ratios less than 1 indicate a greater modeled peak IgG response relative to IgA. Results are presented separately for the NI and NV studies, with GI.1 and GII.4 responses evaluated where available.

Across both studies, model-estimated peak IgA:IgG response ratios were generally greater than 1, indicating modestly larger peak IgA than IgG responses, with little evidence of consistent dose-dependent differences.

## Additional antibody response analyses

### Evaluation of antibody responses following second vaccine dose

The NV study used a two-dose vaccination regimen, with the second dose administered 28 days after the first dose. To evaluate whether the booster dose was associated with a secondary increase in antibody responses, we performed two complementary analyses. First, among participants with both day 28 and day 35 measurements, we compared antibody levels before and after booster administration. For participants with replicate day 35 measurements, an increase was defined as any day 35 measurement exceeding the corresponding day 28 measurement. Second, we identified the timing of each participant's maximum observed antibody measurement to determine whether peak responses consistently occurred after booster administration.

Across antibody types and dose groups, some individual antibody levels increased following the second dose (@tbl-nv-second-dose), but most participants reached their maximum observed antibody response before booster administration (@tbl-nv-peak-1 - @tbl-nv-peak-5). Neither analysis demonstrated a consistent pattern across antibody types, individuals, or dose groups, nor did they support the presence of a consistent population-level secondary peak following booster vaccination.

Additional zoomed-in versions of the individual trajectory plots (@fig-id-nv-model-1 to @fig-id-nv-model-5), focusing on the first 60 days following initial vaccination and denoting day 28 (booster administration) and the maximum observed antibody response, were generated for visual inspection and are available in the GitHub repository.

```{r}
  fit_flextable_to_page()
```

Given the limited sample sizes and sparse sampling around booster administration, we considered a more complex model incorporating a distinct booster-associated peak to be insufficiently identifiable. We therefore applied the same single-peak model structure to both the NV and NI studies. The model allowed for peak responses to occur after the second dose through the inflection point parameter ($K$), when supported by the data. As a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the analyses using a prior on $K$ centered at a median time-to-peak of 30 days. This alternative prior produced qualitatively similar posterior estimates and did not change the study conclusions (@fig-prior-sens-7 - @fig-prior-sens-16).

These analyses do not exclude the possibility that the second dose influenced antibody maintenance or subsequent waning without producing a distinct secondary peak. Such effects could be partially reflected through the estimated decay parameter ($D$). Denser sampling around booster administration would be required to evaluate models that explicitly represent booster-associated changes in antibody induction and waning.

## Sensitivity analyses

### Prior sensitivity analysis

To assess sensitivity to prior specification, we repeated all analyses using broader prior distributions. We doubled the prior standard deviations for the $p$, $g$, $k$, and $d$ parameters. For the inflection point parameter, $k$, we centered the broader prior at $\log(30)$ to test whether the distribution converged to an inflection point corresponding to approximately 30 days after exposure (@fig-prior-sens-1 - @fig-prior-sens-16). This was of interest because of the two-dose vaccination regimen in the NV study, where the second vaccine was administered 28 days after the first. Some quantitative differences were observed for growth rate and time-to-peak estimates and credible intervals in the NI GI.1 HBGA-blocking models and several NV exponential models (@tbl-prior-sens-1 - @tbl-prior-sens-16). @fig-ni-measures-prior-sens and @fig-nv-measures-prior-sens show the model-estimated kinetic measures under models fit with these prior specifications, analogous to the dose-associated measures in the main text. These figures show that the differences were consistent across dose groups and did not alter the relative comparisons among doses or the overall interpretation of the results.

### Censoring bounds

To account for censoring, observations below the assay’s lower limit of detection were treated as interval-censored. On the linear scale, the natural lower bound would be zero, but because antibody levels are modeled on a natural log scale, log(0) is undefined. In the main analysis, we arbitrarily set a lower bound of $10^{-6}$ 

To assess the sensitivity of this choice, we performed additional analyses using a larger lower bound of $10^{-2}$ and a smaller lower bound of $10^{-14}$.

### Decay calculation

The power-law model assumes that antibody waning slows over time, so decay rate is time-dependent. In the main text, we report decay rates evaluated at day 90, defined as the instantaneous rate of change at day 90. As a sensitivity analysis, we also evaluated decay rates at days 60, 180, and 365 to assess whether the choice of evaluation time influenced the interpretation of antibody kinetics.

@fig-ni-pow-decay-days and @fig-nv-pow-decay-days show model-estimated decay rates at days 60, 90, 180, and 365 for the NI and NV studies, respectively. Across all time points, the qualitative patterns were unchanged. Dose-group ordering, relative differences among antibody types, and the overall interpretation of antibody waning remained consistent regardless of the evaluation day.

@fig-peak-decay-days-1year examines the joint relationship between peak response, decay rate, and model-estimated one-year response using decay rates evaluated at days 60, 180, and 365. Similar to the day-90 analyses presented in the main text, higher peak responses across dose groups tended to be accompanied by faster decay, whereas within dose groups peak response and decay rate remained largely independent. Consequently, the interpretation of the relationship between early antibody kinetics and long-term persistence was not sensitive to the specific time point used to summarize the power-law decay rate.

### Baseline normalization

@fig-ni-pow-measures-absolute and @fig-nv-pow-measures-absolute compare model-estimated antibody kinetics expressed relative to baseline (as presented in the main text) with the corresponding absolute antibody titers for the NI and NV studies, respectively. Measures include baseline titer, peak titer, peak response, predicted one-year titer, and predicted one-year response. @fig-absolute-measures-vs and @fig-absolute-peak-decay-1year examine the relationships between growth rate, peak titer, decay rate, and predicted one-year titer using the same framework as Figures 5 and 6 of the main text. Corresponding analyses for GII.4 antibodies are shown in @fig-pow-gii4-absolute-measures-vs and @fig-pow-gii4-absolute-peak-decay-1year.

In the NI study, baseline titers were generally similar across challenge doses for GI.1 HBGA-blocking antibodies, although the 4800 dose group had slightly lower IgA and IgG baselines. Peak HBGA-blocking responses decreased modestly with increasing dose, and this pattern became more apparent when examining absolute peak titers. Although the 4800 dose produced the largest IgA peak response, it had the smallest estimated peak titer. Likewise, although the 4800 dose produced the largest predicted one-year response, absolute one-year titers were similar across dose groups. IgG peak responses were similar across doses, but absolute peak titers for the 4800 dose were lower than those of the other groups. Overall, baseline normalization had little influence on the interpretation of one-year antibody levels.

In the NV study, the 50 and 150 doses had lower baseline GI.1 IgA, GII.4 IgA, and GII.4 IgG titers than the 5 and 15 doses. Peak responses and peak titers showed similar qualitative dose patterns. However, for several antibodies, the 50 dose produced the largest predicted one-year response but among the lowest absolute predicted one-year titers, reflecting differences in baseline antibody levels rather than post-vaccination kinetics.

Across studies, GI.1 baseline titers were broadly comparable between the infection and vaccination cohorts. NI participants generally maintained higher HBGA-blocking antibody titers at one year than NV participants, particularly when we considered absolute titers. Importantly, using absolute titers rather than baseline-relative responses did not change the relationships among kinetic measures. Growth rate remained weakly associated with one-year titers, peak titer remained positively associated, and decay rate remained negatively associated. Peak titer also remained positively associated with decay rate across dose groups, indicating that larger peak responses were generally accompanied by faster waning. In some dose groups, lower peak titers combined with slower waning produced comparable or higher one-year titers.

Overall, expressing antibody kinetics as absolute titers rather than responses relative to baseline introduced only minor differences in interpretation and did not change the principal conclusions. Baseline-relative responses quantify the magnitude of the antibody increase following exposure, whereas absolute titers additionally reflect pre-existing immunity.
